utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you for giving me the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, you know that we started this conversation yesterday. I'm kindly asking you to speak as slowly as possible and I will also try to abide by this, because if we do not follow this procedure, it will not go well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I please pick up where we left off yesterday, and can we also please have 65 ter document 2872, and if it can be enlarged so that numbers can be legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, yesterday you said that at one point you went to a position where you acted as an observer. Can you explain what happened which prompted you to leave the position in your house and the circumstances that you lived in to go to that particular place. Do you know when the army of Republika Srpska was established?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army of Republika Srpska was established in mid-May, sometime between the 12th and the 19th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you had asked another question, and I think this is the problem when you ask more than one question. I was more interested in the first question, which is his explanation as to what prompted him to leave the position in his house and the circumstances that he lived in. What prompted him to go to that particular place? Witness, can you answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't leave my home. I joined the army of Republika Srpska that was established at the time. My motives were to take part in the defence of my property, lives and people with whom I was living.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where did you act as an observer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday I showed point A on the map, and this is where I was deployed as an observer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What were your functions as an observer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My function was to observe the area, to see the deployment of forces, the movement of enemy forces, the establishment of fortifications facing our territory, and to pass on this information to the command in charge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have heard of another type of observer in this case and that's the observer who is sent when mortars are being fired, and I wondered whether he had any of these functions or whether he was simply somebody observing the enemy and passing on reports to his headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was mention, Your Honour, of observers and the witnesses explained this. I exactly wanted to ask the witness to explain what was he observing from his post. That was my intention. But I first wanted to hear that he already at that point had joined the army of Republika Srpska and, of course, I would like to hear his explanation about what he was observing from that post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, when you were deployed at this position, what weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally wasn't issued any weapons. I was issued actually a rifle for my self-defence against any incursions. I also had binoculars, a radio set, a military telephone, a map and a compass.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From that post where you were at the time, what were you able to observe? Can you tell the Judges that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Mojmilo hill was visible from that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Who controlled the Mojmilo hill at the time when you were observing it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, and throughout the war, the Muslim forces controlled the peaks and we had a part of Mojmilo on the slopes facing Nedzarici where our troops were controlling the waterworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear that? The interpreter is asking you to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, I am really asking you: Do not speak fast. Speak slowly. Otherwise nothing will be recorded. For how long were these people deployed next to the waterworks and experienced what you said they experienced?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly up until mid-June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from then on, who took control of these positions on Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exclusively Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark on the map this hill called Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That will be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that this hill, Gavrica Brdo, from which you observed the territory, was approximately 650 metres high. With regard -- with respect to you, do you know the height of Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 680 and 690 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From that position, viewing towards Grbavica and Dobrinja but most of all towards Grbavica and other parts of the city surrounding Grbavica, what were you able to see, if anything?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can't see anything over Mojmilo because Vraca, Debelo Brdo and other places are beyond it. You cannot see anything. You can see only one part of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please slow down. It is completely futile if you speak too fast. So what part of Dobrinja were you able to see?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could see only the frontal parts of buildings in Dobrinja because the viewing angle with respect to distance was very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this part of Dobrinja that you were able to see, how far was it from the airport?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's immediately across the airport and you can see the first buildings there on the line, so the distance would be about 50 metres, up to 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know for how long the airport was under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The airport was handed over to UNPROFOR in order to allow for the arrival of humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us approximately the parts of Dobrinja that you were able to see?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where is the airport?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the line with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then mark Dobrinja with a letter D.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And Mojmilo with a letter M.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far was Gavrica Brdo hill from Mojmilo or, rather, Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately 4 kilometres from Mojmilo, and 2.5 to 3 kilometres from Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were you actually able to see in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually, what I could see were only the frontal parts of Dobrinja and the buildings there, and the rest one could see were just the tops of other buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, after the airport had been handed over to UNPROFOR or, rather, international forces, did any of the officers come to your position at Gavrica Brdo?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Mladic himself used to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Why did he come? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he held meetings with people in Vojkovici, explaining the reasons for handing over the airport. After that, he dropped by our observation post and ordered the other units to take particular care that nothing should happen at the airport. He even said there shouldn't be a stone or a rock thrown at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where the separation lines were between the VRS, with respect to Mojmilo, but can you show us where the separation lines were between the VRS and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, what have you marked with the letter A?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the place at Krtelji and that was the Special Police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the place that had been marked with a G, Gavrici Brdo, as you said, it was facing Mojmilo. What else was it facing?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where Igman is on this map?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not shown here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You can see but a small part of Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the toponym.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was Igman compared to Hrasnica, or, rather, how far was Hrasnica from your observation post?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where is Igman compared to or in relation to Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Igman begins at Hrasnica. That's where the foot is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, from the hill marked with a G, you were observing positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were where?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We observed their lines. Therefore, it was in Donji Kotarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where that is?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There. We could also see parts of Butmir and Cigansko Maselj [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Stop there, please. When you say Cigansko Maselj, a Roma settlement, what are you trying to say? Who resided there?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the beginning of the war, the Roma lived there, who probably had built their houses there illegally. However, the Muslim forces used that to place their recoilless gun and a mortar in their houses, as well as several machine-guns. Therefore, they turned a civilian target into a military one at the expense of the Roma.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the focus of military activity? Can you explain to us what the activities were that were taking place at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't many infantry attacks. They mostly opened fire from artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that go for both sides?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both sides. Of course, an action causes a reaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina usually open their fire from? You were at Gavrica Brdo and Mojmilo and Igman were there, but where did they usually fire from?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From several directions. Usually from Igman, from the Kovaci settlement in Hrasnica; they used mortars there. From the Roma settlement, there was a recoilless gun and a mortar there. The Butmir settlement, there was a mortar group there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am getting there. I'm just waiting for the transcript. There was a group of houses between the airport and Dobrinja. We called them the Fulina houses and they had guns there. And of course from Mojmilo. They were guided by pointers from the top. And they also used machine-guns to target Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, at the outset, what weaponry was there on the side of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we had weaponry. After the JNA had been disbanded and the VRS formed, we assumed positions. There were several tanks and several Pragas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You had a telephone device, as you said. What could you see from the Mojmilo hill and what was the information you passed on to those who were supposed to take action?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the answer that I can give to the Judges. My job was to observe, to follow where the fire was coming from. I had to provide grid reference and forward that to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During those days, were you able to observe something that you could share with us, something that remains etched in your memory?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed something I will never forget. In mid-August, a howitzer began operating at Igman. The calibre was probably 150 millimetres. It is a long-range piece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which year is this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. I did my utmost to try and locate the howitzer. I finally succeeded. I located it at Igman. The exact location is called Radiljavaca [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During those days, were you able to hear something over the radio, something that had to do with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. That's why I knew the calibre, because they boasted in public that a sultan was brought to Igman and that it was brought there by Dajda and that we were going to feel what a 150-millimetre gun actually means in real terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you relay to the people that you were supposed to relay information to?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I provided a grid reference and I awaited some sort of a reply. There was an attempt on our part to destroy the howitzer but we failed. Our range proved too short. The next day, since the Muslims realised that we pinpointed the location and they knew that we were observing from the Gavrica hill, since they had a commanding view from Igman - they were higher than we were - they started with the barrage of shells, an enormous number of shells. I was wounded on that occasion, and the very same shell killed my friend, Nenad Vaskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of injury did you sustain and what happened subsequently?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was seriously injured to my stomach. Basically I had my intestines in my hands. I was also injured to one of my arms and both legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you treated?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first emergency operation was executed at Pale. Since we couldn't go via Zlatiste, I was taken via Tvrdimic, which took three hours. The other operations happened in Belgrade, in their emergency centre. I had another five operations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, how long did the treatment take?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned on the 10th of March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were you able to participate in any observing activities or combat activities for that matter at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was demobilised. May I add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to say that after the first operation at Pale, I was awakened from a coma by the howitzer shots because they were targeting Olovnica and the Presidency at Pale.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The hospital and the Presidency at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between Igman and Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies, about 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the exact name of that 155-millimetre howitzer? You said they called it Sulejman.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sultan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sultan. But what is the military designation?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a Nora.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you concluded your treatment, where did you go? What did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the treatment, and after I spent several months at home, in November I went to Trnovo. It says "November" in the transcript whereas it should be August. I was appointed hotel manager at Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties at Trnovo and for how long did you perform them?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title "manager" didn't mean much at the time, since it had to do with the returning of population to Trnovo and providing accommodation for them, and it was an attempt to regain a semblance of ordinary life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as not to forget, I wanted to go back to the situation we see on the map. We should assign it a Defence Exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, at the time you were at Trnovo working as the manager, what was the situation among the population like?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was critical. Those people had been driven away in 1992 and were now returning to their homes, trying to reconstruct their houses, and they were visibly impoverished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From August 1992 until June 1994. It's within that time. The most pressing issue was food.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me something about the time after that, the summer of 1994? What was happening with you? What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that summer, I stayed with my wife who was pregnant at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's other microphone be turned on as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you turn on the other microphone. The interpreter is having difficulty hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, after that period that you spent with your pregnant wife in the summer of 1994, were you subsequently given some sort of a task? And what was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the needs of the municipality of Ilidza, which was split into two, the eastern and the western part, I was tasked to organise an office that would liaise with UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, with whom did you have contacts most frequently, since you had to do that and since that was your task?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The central office was situated in Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us where that is on the map. Now we have a clean map, 2872. I think I requested this to be saved and I think it has been. If it hasn't been saved, then we can add these new markings. So please show us where Ilidza is and where this central office is.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's here, in the Serbia Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was your office?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My office was in Kasindol. It's here. Here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please mark that with the letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but before we get on to another topic and before we change this map - I imagine that the President would like to intervene as well - but I have a general question to put to you. Telecoms are very important when it comes to the reliability of information that an observer transmits to the command of his unit and as well to the command of the SRK, and of course it's very important to make sure that the orders received by the command be transmitted to the base. So I noticed that the witness had at his disposal a radio as well as a military telephone or field phone; on page 3, line 13 of the transcript, and on page 8, line 24 of the transcript. We once talked about the phone in this courtroom. So I would like to know the following: Could the witness inform me what is the difference between his radio, the radio set in English, and the military phone? And I would like to know if that phone was a land line or was it a mobile phone?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, can you please answer?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll answer that. It's not a difficult question. A radio set is used exclusively in the field, and it's been adjusted for intercepting. The military telephone has only one wire connecting one telephone to another, so basically only two persons can communicate over this phone at a time. A special cable is extended from the centre all the way to the observation post. And that was precisely the reason why I was wounded, because I was in the open and I was laying down this cable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the radio? What kind of a radio did you have? Was it a walkie-talkie? Was it something else? What kind of a system was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a standard military radio device that one carries on one's back, and it was used very rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my last question to you: So you were in contact with your command and you knew that your command was in regular contact with the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber is troubled by the relevance of this evidence. We have been listening to this witness for over an hour and we haven't heard much that is relevant to the charges. You must bring the witness to evidence that relates to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I only wanted to describe the general circumstances in which everything started, and on account of what the witness was saying these questions can be interesting for other witnesses as well, as pointed out by His Honour Judge Mindua. This witness's evidence should demonstrate the situation in the indictment period with regard to the people living in that area, what shortages they had to endure, what fears they had to endure. As somebody who in this particular period of time was involved exclusively in civilian affairs and cooperation with UNPROFOR, he's a well-suited person to tell us about the condition in which the people were living at the time, particularly in the indictment time period, and the problems that existed then even with regard to weapons and everything else. He can also tell us what was happening in the period and the counts in the indictment against Dragomir Milosevic. So he can tell us quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But not all so, I mean, that is what he is to tell us about. It seems to me to be less important, the conditions in which the people were living. We are interested in evidence that will help us to determine the innocence or guilt of the accused. Peripheral matters will not help us very much. So if he has evidence about the charges in the indictment, let us hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the central point here was the intention of the VRS to terrorise the people living in the parts of Sarajevo controlled by the ABiH. This witness can tell us very much about the fears and the plight of his people who lived there as a result of the incidents cited in the indictment, including the people who were living in the area under the VRS control in Sarajevo itself, and what kind of suffering they had to endure, which were not at all different from everything that was happening in those places: Who was holding these hills, who was deployed on these hills, which is the basic foundation of this indictment; that is to say, that one army had its positions on the hills and relentlessly fired at civilians in order to instill terror in them. The Defence wants to prove that it was quite the opposite, that it was not true, and to provide evidence, even through the evidence presented by the Prosecution, about who was on the hills. The Defence believes that in 80 per cent of cases it has been shown who was on the hills and the VRS was at the foot hills doing nothing other than defending their positions and being compelled to respond to what was happening in military terms. Therefore, this witness was living with civilians --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear that evidence. If he has evidence about who was on the hills, that's very relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is precisely the point that I have reached, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let us get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, we have come to the point when you began working with UNPROFOR on humanitarian aid. In order to address the issue that I have been warned about - and I have to comply with the Court's request and shed light on this - can you first show me or, rather, explain where these two offices were. What was the most pressing matter in those days? How did you obtain medicines, for example?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The most important problem was medicines and control and prevention of contagious diseases. The warehouses were at the airport, and if a delivery was to be made in the western part of Ilidza, we had to go around town for about 100 kilometres in order to get these medicines. And that was precisely the reason for setting up this office, in order to cut short the route of delivery.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So where did you take over the medicines?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the office was set up, the medicines were delivered directly to the hospital in Kasindol from the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any reason for you to go to Ilidza? Because the headquarters was there during the period that you were involved in these duties.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, it is only logical for me that I had to go there on a weekly basis and submit reports on my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So which route did you have to take? Can you show the Judges on the map, without drawing it.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first had to go to Pale, then Sumbulovac, then Vogosca, and then Ilidza. So I had to take a round-about road through the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can we please save this map and admit it as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I add something about the map? I made a mistake when I marked my office. It was actually here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark it with a letter D?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this map be admitted as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D224, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in order to reach Ilidza, were you able to go across the airport?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go, which route did you take, and who was dominating the hills that you had to pass by in order to reach Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to pass from Kasindol through Dobrinja and I had a problem already there. Then Mojmilo, Trebevic, Colina Kapa. Then there was a safe part of the road to Grdonj, and then descending down to Vogosca exposed one to constant fire from Hum and Vogosca, and then the situation was rather stable up to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what did it look like from Vogosca to Ilidza? How long was that particular section?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps about 10 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During your travel, who was in control of the elevations all around?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslims at Hum and at Zuc, in the direction of Mijatovica Kosa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly but I think it was sometime in August 1994, at least that's what I'd heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation at the time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't get the last part of the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The heavy weapons had been withdrawn by February. This had been organised by UNPROFOR. This was a relatively peaceful period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say "peaceful," what exactly are you trying to say?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that there were no serious operations at the time. There was a cease-fire on. And there were just sporadic incidents. No more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When was it that you had this peaceful period in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember because of the school year. I think it went on until about October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What is it about the school year that you're trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I did. I looked after the local population. Children went to school, for example, in Vojkovici. Vojkovici. And when this began, in about October 1994, the offensives, there were regular activities by browning from Igman on the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in your capacity as a humanitarian worker?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked UNPROFOR to set up some sort of protection for the school building, to go there themselves and guard the building. Secondly, I asked for fuel for the ferrying of peoples. We couldn't just leave them there in the school building under fire. The idea being to take them across to the barracks. I then had a meeting with the airport commander, Colonel Oberto, who approved this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which officers of the army of Republika Srpska did you talk to about this, the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, those were liaison officers. That was my only communication with the army. There was no need for any other form of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you say the offensive was launched or, rather, the fighting began in October. What did it look like? Where exactly did this go on?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this area, the focus was near Trnovo. There was fierce fighting going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps at the time hear anything that reminded you of your own experience back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was touring the positions held by our soldiers, along with members of an association called the Serb Sisters. It's a women's association. My task was to take them to see the soldiers, bring them food and encouragement. I then heard those same howitzers or maybe similar ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness a document, DD001737.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You've been speaking about these weapons, but please have a look at this document. Who was it produced by, what date does it bear, what's it in reference to, and, lastly, who signed it? Can you have a look, please. Sir, Mr. Maunaga, it's a rather short document. Can you read the date, the substance and the signatory, in that order, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 18th December 1994, signed by General Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what's it in reference to?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that it's in reference to precisely what I have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What exactly?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: 152 howitzers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Which you heard firing again at this time; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the sound of the howitzer being fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty, we are still considering the relevance of much of this evidence, and it really goes to the root of the Defence case because, of course, it's not enough really to show that the Serbs were also suffering. But I believe what the Defence is saying is not just that the Serbs were suffering but that the terror with which you have charged their client was caused by the ABiH themselves. And so he's bringing evidence, for example, this order by General Delic, which has to do with the placement of howitzers, to show that the ABiH were in a position to inflict terror. I find it a very, very difficult question because unless I can reconcile the issue of the relevance, much of the Defence case will remain very questionable. But I observe that the Prosecutor does not raise any questions about relevance and, indeed, cross-examines on the evidence that has been adduced. But I would like to get the views of Mr. Waespi and yourself, or you, since your handling this witness, on this issue which the Chamber is finding very, very difficult to reconcile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have not raised a relevancy objection so far because the Chamber has been asking questions concerning the relevancy of the testimony and so I considered any objections or submissions that I would have made to have been redundant, quite frankly. With regard to the line of defence that you outlined in your question to me, I have not heard that evidence. I have heard evidence that the Serbian population suffered. The Prosecution has never denied that the Serbian population suffered. That was the first half of what you outlined. The second half of what you outlined, however, that the terror with which the accused is charged was in fact caused by the ABiH, I have not heard evidence coming from the Defence regarding that. So far this morning, with all respect to the witness who I know went through a terrible experience in the war, he has testified that he, a soldier in uniform, was wounded while performing a military task. This was from, he submits, a 152-millimetre howitzer. We now are shown an order from about two years later saying that a 152-millimetre howitzer is to be taken from some unspecified place - it is not set out in the order - undergo some unspecified modifications - it is not set out in the order - and then taken back to the place from whence it came. I cannot connect those dots into a colourable submission that terror was caused by the ABiH and that is but one example. I do not -- I do not contest that if evidence of the sort you described was coming in, it would have relevance. My submission is simply that it is not coming in. With regard to the Prosecution's cross-examinations, without getting into matters of strategy, I would say that we cross-examine on those points - speaking for myself, I think I have to limit it to that; Mr. Waespi might be able to speak team-wide - cross-examine on those points that do have relevance and so, for example, I think that most of my cross-examinations have been centred upon the question of who controlled the hilltops. We've probably spent more time on that than on any other individual topic, although there have been some other things that have come up with regard to the testimony of other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber really wants to understand your case, and we are struggling to find out just how the evidence that you are now suggesting to us can support what we believe is your case. Just a short while ago, the President once again expressed the views of the Chamber of what we think it is that you are trying to prove to us, and if the President's interpretation and the Chamber's interpretation of this is correct, then I have to ask you just how is it that, for instance, this order by General Delic can show that the terror was really caused by the ABiH. I have difficulties in understanding that, and I kindly ask you to help me out, to understand better how this evidence can support the view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, Your Honours, the Chamber, perhaps the best way to explain this would be to use the present example. You have witness Drazen Maunaga before you. At the beginning of the war he experienced what he experienced. He described that for our benefit. I did not mean to adduce those very documents. I'm sure you trust this witness. You see what this is about. And now you have the same person. At one point in time there had been a lull; there had not been many clashes. Even international observers - I'm not going back to that now - had been saying that by October it had been relatively peaceful. This is also in some of the OTP exhibits and I'm not going into everything else that we the Defence have been talking about. You have this witness at this point in time. The weapons were moved to a different location and now he hears these weapons firing again. This person before you hears the same thing again. How is it possible for this person not to experience stress, fear, perhaps for his own life? What I'm trying to prove is this: Firstly, the key issues regarding who was holding which positions, I am convinced the Defence will succeed in showing many things in a different light than they were presented in the Galic trial. It's precisely about the atrocities suffered by the civilian population because of the fighting on both sides. The best indicator is a person like the present witness who experienced this himself. You can use the presence of this witness to help you realise what the fears were that were involved in a conflict like that, especially those fears that prevailed among the people between May and the end of the war, during the large-scale BH army offensive and the NATO bombing. Those fears prevailed. And I'm not going into other aspects of those fears which is something that we shall be trying to prove. So when we speak of terror, this is something that's difficult to distinguish. This sort of situation creates suffering on the part of all citizens, such as the present witness. I could have brought hundreds of witnesses but there is no time for that. It's that simple. I have only produced a handful of witnesses, such as the present one, to testify to these matters. But I hope the Defence will be successful in showing that they too -- well, that's at least what I believe, of course. I'm not the one who can claim that this has been finally resolved or not. What the cases looked like that were presented are pattern cases, what exactly what was going on, even those 30 or so cases, beyond a reasonable doubt. That when we talk about terror, there can be no distinction made between fears felt by any person alive. Why would a nation inflict something like this upon themselves, hurt themselves and hurt others, too? Regardless of the historical, strategic and other circumstances, these people in late 1994, 1995, 1996, whatever was going on, whatever their desires were at the time, had no urge whatsoever to launch into any sort of action whatsoever, especially as the only objective allegedly was to target civilians. You will be hearing other witnesses. This witness is the best example for you what it means to own a weapon such as this one that has a range of 30 kilometres and you actually listen to it while it's flying through the air. This is just one piece of evidence. We've been able to track down a lot of evidence like this. This is a sure sign of sowing fear among one's own population. Those citizens of Bosnia who were under the control of the BH army, maybe they didn't hear a weapon like this being used but it could have targeted them too. This sort of weapon, this sort of firing, caused fear on both sides of the ethnic divide. So I think this should be something for you to judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We will take into consideration what you have said. I hope by the end of your case I will understand it better, but I think at this moment we should move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We have four minutes before the break. We'll admit the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D225, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, what happened at the end of this time that you were talking about, August, December, the offensive? So, as I said before, what happened at the end?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a ceasefire sometime in December, late December, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about this time period? I'm not sure how long it went on for. Can you tell us that first, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a cease-fire that we felt was some sort of a preparation for a new offensive that would eventually be launched against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you mean that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went on until sometime in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you use that lull for your humanitarian work? What were you actually able to do during that period, in terms of, for example, food or firewood?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We brought supplies to families. We made sure they were safe throughout the winter. UNPROFOR gave us a hand. We took supplies to hospitals. There were infections because of the surplus of garbage. Different sorts of infectious diseases were rife, and they helped us a lot with that. We also brought water to the lower slopes around Sarajevo, especially because there were many refugees living there who had escaped from the fighting. We also went to Kasindol, but those slopes had no running water and obviously this required assistance by UNPROFOR. In addition to food shipments, it was also about actually distributing these shipments. So that is mostly what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have very few questions left. If we could have the break now for me to go through my questions again to see if I can drop any, maybe that might cut the whole thing short. And it is half past 10.00, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, not quite, but we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, perhaps we can go over a couple of things before we finish so that you can explain something to the Judges. You said that there was a lull between December and June. When you said that, what was the first thing that came to your mind?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant to say that there were no intensive combat activities in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: During that period, did you have contact with the population? For example, did you go down to Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I moved about all those parts, and every second or third day I went to Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, what did Grbavica look like in terms of layout of its geographic position? How did you feel down there?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grbavica is in a depression in relation to the Muslim positions. One could always hear small-arms fire; therefore, one always moved around Grbavica with fear. The people who lived there knew of certain routes that they were supposed to take, but unless you were familiar with those, you were risking your life.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, can you tell me whether you ever managed to reach the population of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I often went to Ilidza. However, I didn't dare to go to Nedzarici, although I had friends and family there. I didn't know a way in and how to move around that part, because that part was very exposed to combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you talked to the people at Grbavica and Nedzarici, what would they usually tell you?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was particularly interesting was that the fear was present all the time, but it intensified during that period, because the people had a feeling that the other side was gaining in strength and that they were getting ready to drive them away from those parts. An additional factor was the stories one could hear from the people who came from inside the city, who could tell about the atrocities in the city, about torture, and people disappearing overnight. And then they would always ask me, since I had contacts with foreigners, whether there was any possibility for me to secure a visa for them or to do anything so that they could be -- they could leave the area. And the same goes for all of the parts in the eastern territories around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in June, since you mentioned June a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June there was a large offensive in the area of Trnovo and Nisici.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did all that look like?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot put it in strictly military terms but the intensity of fighting was great, and I know that because everyone who was able to fight, all able-bodied people, were included in the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you, as someone who dealt in civilian affairs, did you have any specific tasks at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the offensive began, my contact with the UNPROFOR and international organisations ceased. Therefore, I was assigned a new role, to organise civilian protection, because it was a matter of survival in that area, and all able-bodied people were supposed to take part in the defence. We even had to count on the elderly and women to harvest and to cut grass, to secure firewood for the winter, for had we not done that we would have put our own existence into question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did that last?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted all the way until the Dayton agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened after the Dayton Accords? Did you manage to return to your apartment in the centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I guess the people living there wouldn't like to see me come back because I knew a lot about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the people of Grbavica, Nedzarici, Dobrinja, Ilidza, the people who used to live there?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Dayton Accords, they all left those areas because they feared the new authorities that were to be appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since your house was in Kasindol, it is close to Vojkovici. Concerning the people who used to live there, did they sustain any civilian or military casualties? Can you tell us in brief?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I made surveys; I collected data to provide to the international organisations, to be able to show what the number of casualties was, what the number of those who had their limbs amputated due to the war was. Therefore, I know that in Kasindol there were about 130 killed and some 20 civilian casualties; in Vojkovici, around 150 killed and around 30 civilian casualties. I don't have information for Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maunaga.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This concludes my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maunaga.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, my name is John Docherty. I'm one of the lawyers on the Prosecution side of this case. I know that the events that you are testifying to are very difficult for you, but it is necessary that I ask you a few questions but I don't think this will be all that terribly long. If you have any question about what I am saying or if you don't understand, please ask me to clear it up rather than guessing at what I may be asking you. Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to talk with you a little bit about your military career, Mr. Maunaga. What was the highest rank that you held in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I held no rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You were a private soldier?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A regular soldier, a private.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, what company you were in? And then just so you know where I'm going, I'm going to go up the chain and ask you what battalion you were in, what brigade you were in. So let's start at the bottom. What company were you a member of?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the reconnaissance company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And was the reconnaissance company assigned to any particular battalion; and if it was, could you tell us, number 1, which battalion and, number 2, the name of the commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact hierarchy but I think my company was under direct command of the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And when you say "the brigade," is that the 1st Sarajevo Infantry Brigade or is it some other brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And at the time that you were a member of the 1st Sarajevo Infantry Brigade, who was its commanding officer, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then lastly, sir, when you did your national service in the Yugoslav People's Army, what was the rank that you held and what was the kind of duty that you performed?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a private, trained as a scout.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So much the same type of duties that you later performed with the SRK when you were on the hill of Gavrica.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. That's the training that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: As a private soldier, you had duties to perform, probably quite important duties, but you yourself were obviously not in daily contact with the senior leadership of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Am I correct in that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had no contact with them, or if there was any, it was seldom. I only had to relay information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And in order to relay information, you described the equipment that you had up on the hill and I'll just go through that again and ask you to affirm that this is correct. You had a pair of binoculars; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: A map?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: A compass?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And for communications, you had a military telephone and you also had a radio set. Do I have that right, Mr. Maunaga?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And is the reason that you had two different means of communicating, both a military telephone and a radio set, because it was important that your information get to the commanders behind your position?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the information that you gathered concerning the dispositions of the army facing you were, as far as you know, sent back up a chain of command to be used by military decision-makers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you came on duty each time that you did, did you test your radios -- your radio and your military telephone to make sure that they were working properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is one of the basic tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And the information that you gathered, who did it go to? Who were you communicating to?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the communications centre with the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You said "with the command." With the command of what? Of the brigade? Of some other unit?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The brigade command of the 1st Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so far as you know, the brigade command then used the information you gave them, together with other things, of course, to fight the war and to decide which troops would go where, which weapons would go where, and other sorts of military decisions; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And during your time with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you observe it to have a properly functioning chain of command in which more senior officers gave orders to less senior officers who in turn gave orders to private soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't bother to follow how the chain worked but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you ever see any indication that the chain was not working?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was in -- when it was in the JNA, was the old 4th Corps of the Yugoslav People's Army; is that correct, Mr. Maunaga?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Are you aware that the -- are you aware that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps took over many of the military assets and many of the officers of the 4th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that the equipment that was left by the JNA was taken over. I don't know about any officers, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you joined the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps in 1992, who was the commanding officer of the corps, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And General Galic was a career JNA officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is a bit leading. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, it's all right to lead on cross-examination, but I understand your concern. You were wounded and out of the army by late in 1992, am I right about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity before coming to testify to read over the amended indictment, the document that brings the charges in this case?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: If you haven't had an opportunity to read over the indictment, are you aware from any other source that the charges in this case concern a period of time beginning approximately two years after you left the corps?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it pertains to the period of command of General Milosevic, since he is the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you know that General Milosevic was in command of the corps beginning in about August of 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So while you were in the army, you did not have daily contact with senior decision-makers, and after you left the army is when the period of time concerning this case begins; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you were giving your direct testimony, you testified with regard to a hill called Mojmilo, and I have a couple of questions concerning Mojmilo. First of all, did I understand you properly, did you say that the SRK or the VRS, as part of controlling the lower slopes, also controlled the municipal waterworks?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a certain period, the VRS did control not the municipal but the city waterworks, rather. It was until June. And then we withdrew our soldiers from there because they were being killed there regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: When you say "the city waterworks," is the city in "city waterworks" the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see in the transcript that June is mentioned, and that is what the witness mentioned, but the Prosecutor's question was -- well, I think it had to do with the year. So we have June but of what year?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What year is this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Now, also with regard to Mojmilo, you have not read the amended indictment in this case, but are you aware, Mr. Maunaga, from maybe some other source that the sniping incidents alleged in this case are in several clustered areas within the city of Sarajevo? And I'll just mention two of them: Marin Dvor and Sedrenik. Let's start with Marin Dvor. Do you know that area from the time that you spent living in the city of Sarajevo? Do you know what I mean when I say "Marin Dvor"?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know Marin Dvor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And what about Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vaguely. I went there very rarely, maybe once or twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And do you know that Sedrenik is below a hill called Sharpstone?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not particularly familiar with that area. I didn't go there often. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: All right. If you're not familiar with it, we won't ask -- I won't ask you questions about that area. But with regard to Marin Dvor, do you know the S-curve in the tram tracks that's roughly in front of the Holiday Inn on Zmaja od Bosne?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that curve.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And from Mojmilo, a rifleman, a sharp-shooter, could not hit that S-curve because there are buildings in the way; isn't that correct? In particular the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never looked at this part from Mojmilo and I think it's far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Just to make clear, you would say that Marin Dvor is far away from Mojmilo?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is far away but it's within range.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Okay. It's within range, as long as there is a clear shot from there; is that correct? And also, that you are saying you don't know whether there is a clear shot or not, never having yourself looked.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, you also, in your direct evidence, talked about the period of time after you left the army, when you were moving about from area to area, and in particular, I want to talk with you about the route that you described and marked on the map going sort of around the perimeter of the city. Do you know the chunk of direct testimony I'm referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help. Do you know the road that runs from Lukavica to Pale?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And it may be because I misunderstood your direct testimony, but did you testify that in moving around the city, and in particular in going to Ilidza, you had to drive all the way around town and I think part of your route was on the Lukavica-to-Pale road? Does that help and did I understand properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And you were able, on roads, to travel all the way around town from Lukavica to Pale and then on around the north end of Sarajevo and down into Ilidza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all called a road. However, one had to take a forest road to get to Ilidza and these were very inaccessible roads. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it was easy, but I'm saying that it was possible and that you did it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible but with a great risk. I said parts and sections of the roads were constantly exposed to activities and the risks were high.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And on the southern side of town, where the Lukavica-to-Pale segment is, what I want to concentrate on, that road runs along a ridge line that is to the south of Sarajevo; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And that road, keeping that road open was very important to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, was it not, because if that road was cut, physical communication between Lukavica and Pale would have been impossible.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And, in fact, throughout the war, other than occasional raids by the ABiH that were repulsed, that road was never permanently cut by the ABiH, was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And as you drive along that road, you are fairly high up, with a commanding view over the city of Sarajevo. And again I'm referring to the Lukavica-to-Pale segment. Is that correct, Mr. Maunaga?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not exactly. There is a very short section from which Sarajevo can be seen. Otherwise, you pass behind a hill or the visibility is reduced because of the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Two follow-on questions to that, sir. First of all, the section from which Sarajevo can be seen, could you tell us where that section is, please? I'm not going to ask to you mark on a map. Just describe it in words, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a section after Zlatiste up to the Osmice curve or even a shorter section. I didn't look upon Sarajevo from that point, never during the war. I just tried to pass as quickly as possible along that section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And then my second follow-on question, Mr. Maunaga, deals with the lowered visibility from either hills or from the woods. During your time in the army, did you ever -- either the JNA or the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you ever get trained on mortars?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Even if you weren't trained on mortars, did you ever hear mortars referred to as indirect-fire weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what indirect fire is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Indirect fire, Mr. Maunaga, would mean that the mortar crew does not need to see their target in order to fire at it because the mortar shell goes up in the air on a parabolic curve and then comes back down to earth, and as long as they have an observer to radio back corrections to the fall of a shot, they can engage a target without seeing it. Do you agree that a mortar crew can shoot at things, in fact can hit things, that they cannot see?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that, and that is basically how they operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, I think the last thing I want to speak with you about this morning is the airport. You remember that you gave testimony that General Ratko Mladic came to, was it, your position, or is this something that you heard about, and talked about shooting at the airport? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came to our position to warn us not to even think about shooting or even throwing a stone. And there was no shooting because it was a VRS position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: So when was it that General Mladic -- I don't think you gave this in your direct testimony. When was it that General Mladic gave this speech?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in July. I don't know the exact date, but I think it coincides with the date when the airport was handed over, or maybe a day before that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And so when you say "July," the handover of the airport was in July of 1992. Was it around then?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Did you hear General Mladic yourself or did you hear about what he had said from other people?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I want to explore for a moment, Mr. Maunaga, how that was put into practice. First of all, are you aware that during the trial of General Galic, there was evidence of shooting from SRK positions of civilians seeking to cross the airport? Have you heard that before?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And are you aware that the allegations are that that came from various SRK-controlled hills around the airport?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I don't think there was any activity aimed at the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Could we see Prosecution Exhibit 667, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, on the screen in front of you there is a document. On the right-hand side it's in B/C/S. Is it big enough that you can read it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Mr. Maunaga, just take a minute, read it over, and when you're ready to answer a couple of questions about it, just let me know. And I'm particularly interested in the first three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, this is from 1994. I really have nothing to do with this and I have no knowledge of this kind of military information. I was involved in civilian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Right. I called for this document, Mr. Maunaga, because you said a few minutes ago that, "I don't think there was any activity aimed at the airport." Do you see the paragraph that begins, "Through contacts with UNPROFOR representatives, we have obtained information that in the Ilidza area, they spotted four Bofors, anti-aircraft guns."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness already said that he had no military role in that period, that he was involved in civilian affairs. What he said about the period while he was at the observation post refers to the first half of 1992. About this period, he says that he has no information about military affairs; therefore, he cannot give evidence on this because he knows nothing about these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: May I respond, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect, Mr. Tapuskovic's submission misses the point. We have had evidence from this witness that General Mladic gave direction that the airport was not to be fired upon. I don't know that the witness said that there was any time limit upon that injunction. I now have a document indicating that there were in fact weapons along the axis of flight of UNPROFOR aircraft landing at the Butmir airport, which is the Sarajevo airport in the Butmir neighbourhood, and I think it's perfectly appropriate to put it to the witness. If the witness doesn't know, the witness doesn't know, but I don't see any bar to putting this to the witness in light of the evidence he's given concerning General Mladic's speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Nor do I. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And Mr. Maunaga, the pending question was: Do you see the paragraph beginning, "Through contacts with UNPROFOR representatives, we have obtained information that in the Ilidza area they spotted four Bofors, anti-aircraft guns, deployed along the axis of the flight path of UNPROFOR aircraft landing at the Butmir airport." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: A Bofors gun is a 20-millimetre anti-aircraft weapon; is that correct? Do you know that from your time in the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct. A Bofors gun is a 40-millimetre single-barrelled gun used on ships.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, I think it's safe to say that if they are near the Sarajevo airport, they are probably not being used for naval purposes. They can certainly be modified -- be pressed into service to shoot at other things; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can fire at other things. It shouldn't be mounted on a ship. You can put it on a tree or on a stump.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And this is a document that comes from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I see in the letterhead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
