utterances.text: The Sarajevo airport is in the area of Sarajevo, the district, the neighbourhood, called Butmir; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: And having these weapons in the landing path at Butmir airport is not consistent with what you say General Mladic told you on that day back in 1992, is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether these operations and actions took place. I can say that a majority of the runway from both ends was held by the Muslim forces, so I don't understand who was firing. You're asking me details and I'm telling you that I don't know anything about military affairs. They had Dobrinja on the one side and Butmir on the other side and there was a tunnel underneath.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: You say that you don't know if these guns were used. You testified, I believe, that guns and ammunition were precious commodities in the SRK. Did you talk about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about that. I'm not saying anything about that. What I don't know I'm not going to speak about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Well, let me put it to you this way and perhaps this is something you do know: Was the SRK so rich in weaponry and ammunition that four Bofors guns could be put somewhere and not used?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. First of all, I don't know if they existed at all. I don't know. And secondly, even if they had been deployed, I don't know if they were used. Through my contacts with UNPROFOR, I never received such a protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President, that may be all the questions I have. Could I have one moment to check my notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Docherty?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Maunaga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I put a last question to you, and that is a question that comes out of your testimony about the city waterworks. The reason I'm asking is that we have heard that it was difficult not only for the population living within Sarajevo but also for the population living outside Sarajevo to actually get water. We have evidence that water trucks had to be driven into Sarajevo to provide fresh water to the population living there. So my question is: What was actually the function of the waterworks at Mojmilo which you referred to? Did that waterwork control the access of fresh water to the city of Sarajevo or to the local region, both within the confrontation lines and also outside the confrontation lines? Or were there several waterworks around the city and so you would have to close all of them in order to prevent the people from inside or even outside Sarajevo to get fresh water? What was the function of the waterworks at Mojmilo specifically? Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sure. I was dealing with that issue for a while because the water problem was an obvious problem throughout the area. What we are looking at Mojmilo was no waterworks. There were reservoirs from Ilidza to Mojmilo used for the irrigation of the lower lying town areas. There are several waterworks that enter Sarajevo from other areas. One is from Jahorina Bistrica, the other is from Tilava - there is a tunnel through Mojmilo - and the third is Bacevo and the reservoirs at Mojmilo. It is from that water reservoir that both the Serb and Muslim part of town got their water. There was an attempt being made throughout to supply sufficient amounts of water to both, since these were mutually dependent things. If one party had no water, then the other party had no water either. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It does in part because my next question would be: Then what happened actually to the waterworks or to the reservoirs in Mojmilo? Were they emptied and never refilled or the tubes that let the water down, were they destroyed? What happened to the Mojmilo reservoir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For a brief while, they were under the control of the army or, rather, being guarded to keep anything from happening to them. So the army held that responsibility up until June 1992. And the waterworks remained in operation, in operational order, throughout the war. It was never destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So are you saying that at least the areas which were provided with water from the Mojmilo reservoirs, that those areas at least, they had water throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there was sufficient water but the waterworks remained intact, and it was under the control of their army. It was probably a problem to do with pumps, in terms of water capacity and whether it could actually get sufficient amounts of water across to Mojmilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which then transforms into the question that I put to you before; namely, were the reservoirs in Mojmilo filled with water during the war, from 1992 to 1994-5? Do you know? If you don't know, then please just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know everything but I know that they were operational. Once they'd filled them enough, probably there was sufficient water to get supplies through to everyone. The water problem wasn't resolved before Dayton. We ourselves didn't have sufficient water supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No. I know it was hard for both parties. Thank you very much, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, speaking of water, His Honour Judge Harhoff asked you about outside Sarajevo, what the problem was. Where is Grbavica, Nedzarici, Dobrinja? Where are those?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So there was a water problem, for example, where the Presidency is. Was there a water problem at Grbavica at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But let me go back to what you were cross-examined on by the OTP. So you head out from Lukavica. How long would it take you to reach that small area and by what route from which you could see Sarajevo, from which there was a view of Sarajevo, the road to Pale, wherever you were? What was it like in relation to the lie of the land, and where exactly does that road go?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road goes below Vraca, Miljevici, and then the bend.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Below Vraca, below Miljevici, all right. But I'm asking you in terms of the lie of the land, where do you go? All these places that you pass on the way, do you have a view of Sarajevo, Grbavica, or any other section of Sarajevo from those places?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no views along that road except for that very small section that was constantly under fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about while you were at that observation post, that brief time, what you explained to us previously? Did you ever take that road at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you passed this small section from which you could see Sarajevo, and where do you get to next?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a wooded area next, but you couldn't see anything. From Colina Kapa you could see the road and they kept firing away at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long is the road through the woods that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one under fire or the entire route?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The entire route through the woods.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Something else about one of the questions that you were asked by the OTP. From that observation post at which you were, were you able to observe a single position in the city of Sarajevo itself, Grbavica, for example, or any other section of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From where you were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What was your answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please not speak at the same time as the witness? The interpreters are unable to hear the witness as he answers the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic and the witness, don't overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked him whether he could see Grbavica or any other area of Sarajevo and he said no, not a single one. That's what he said. He said, "I did not see a single area of the city itself." That's what he said and it wasn't recorded. I can tell you because I understand the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, only to make things clear. When one says, "the city itself," I believe that what the witness said would be rather translated by "downtown." I'm not a language expert but I believe that it's not quite the same thing, the city itself and downtown or centre. So what Mr. Maunaga said was "centre de la ville" in French, so "uzi dio grada" in B/C/S, or "downtown," as I would say, in English. It may be that these are only nuances but sometimes they do change things dramatically, because part of our case is also not to make any difference between, say, Grbavica as part of the downtown area, centre de la ville de Sarajevo and, say, Marin Dvor. This is why we are very sensitive to these issues related to translation. And here again, I can't -- I don't know how my own words are being translated, of course. It may be that there are two Judges who understand me in French and I'm really -- I'm keen for the Presiding Judge understanding me, too. I want things to be understood by the Defence and also by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. You say that the witness referred to downtown or the city centre. Let's see now whether Mr. Docherty has another nuance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I don't know if I have a nuance, Mr. President. What I have is an objection to the question. Mr. Tapuskovic's question, beginning on page 49, line 1: "Something else about one of the questions that you were asked by the OTP. From that observation post at which you were, were you able to observe," and so forth and so on. Mr. President, I did not ask him about sight-lines from his observation post; I asked him about sight-lines from Mojmilo; I asked him about the view from the Lukavica-to-Pale road. And I'll also add that in his direct examination, the witness was asked about this and said that he could see Dobrinja, which is in contradiction to the answer he just gave. But my objection is that this was not raised on cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you saying that -- well, it wasn't raised in the way that Mr. Tapuskovic says it was raised but it may have been raised in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: No, my point is stronger. The question that he is asking now relates to a subject that was not raised at all in cross-examination, not in one way or another. He's asking him about sight-lines from his observation post. I did not ask him about that. His observation post was south of the airport. I asked him about the Lukavica-to-Pale road. That's miles away. I asked him about Mojmilo hill. That's also a long way away. And also Mr. Tapuskovic did ask in direct examination about what he could see from that observation post and I'll just submit that the witness gave a different answer. He said he could see Dobrinja. Now he's saying he couldn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You didn't ask about the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I did not ask about sight-lines from the observation post, no, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, no, not sight-lines from the observation post. I'm asking you: Did you not ask questions about the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I asked him what equipment he had in the observation post, and we went through map and compass and telephone and so forth and so on, and I don't remember any other questions about the observation post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it seems we have two issues, one of translation and one more substantive. Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one thing you should bear in mind when you deliberate, what I'm trying to ask is about the question because the OTP asked about indirect firing and information on indirect firing by shells, and that if any information obtained from him could be used on other targets, something along these lines, an interesting question by the OTP. Whether the observation post could get information about indirect firing, along these lines I think it is highly appropriate for me to deal with this. Could he give any sort of information for indirect firing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness, Mr. Maunaga, what could you see from the observation post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could see Mojmilo hill, Dobrinja, the settlement known as Dobrinja, the buildings more to the front only. I could see the airport, Donji Kotarac, the beginning of Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, Hrasnica and Igman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, could you provide any sort of information, given your location, that could be used for indirect firing at targets? Talking about the centre of town, the downtown area, the city itself, whichever you like.

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was certainly in no position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the radio device you were using? Did that device make it possible for you to retrieve information?

utterances.speaker: DRAZEN MAUNAGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We hardly ever used radio communications. It was only once when the phone lines were disrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I will be allowed this next question but it's about this: Did you hear anything about what the Sarajevo media were saying about how somebody from the positions held by the army of Republika Srpska was firing at targets inside the city itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOCHERTY
utterances.text: I object to that question as beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, you did receive very serious injuries during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is the state of your health now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm handicapped. I'm an invalid. I have health problems with my stomach and with my arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, the Chamber sympathises with you and we wish you good health. Your evidence has been concluded. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish to thank the Presiding Judge and the Chamber for your patience and your trust in me as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Goran Kovacevic, but before he's brought in, if we could please deal with a number of procedural matters that will be raised by my colleague? It's about some documents, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. I would like to talk about some documents that were filed as ID documents, documents that were filed and that obtained an identification number because there was no translation. Those documents are translated now and this is why -- or, rather, I would like to rectify something. Some documents are translated. One document that had obtained an ID number, D00206, that document had obtained an identification number because it did not have a translation, but I would like to ask if this document could be filed as evidence, as Defence evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I gave the number right. D00260.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I just see from the entry that it's a combat report dated 20th June 1995 by ABiH Brigadier Fikret Prevljak, and I need to see the exhibit. If the only issue was translation, then we don't have an objection to the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That was the issue, translation. We admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document marked for identification as D206 becomes Exhibit D206.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to mention that with regard to the documents that are already admitted as Defence exhibits, such as D82, D83 and D160, as well as D69, these documents were also not translated, but we have now received the translation of these documents and those translations are in the e-court system. They are entered into the e-court system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, we will just do a little check to ensure that translation was the issue, and a little later on, we'll give the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, once again, I do not know if I was clear. The last four documents that I mentioned, these documents are already admitted as evidence. They were already admitted into evidence, but we are requesting that you take knowledge of the fact that the translation is entered into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. So they are already exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Goran Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. You may begin, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please state your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Goran Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, I would like to ask you to speak slowly and to pay attention to the cursor on the screen, because once it has stopped it means that the interpretation of my question had been completed. And if you pause, it will make us move more efficiently through the examination. Mr. Kovacevic, you were born on the 9th of December 1964.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in Sarajevo, in the part which at that time was called Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You completed your elementary and high school in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You worked at the Pretis factory in Vogosca until the outbreak of the conflict; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, could you explain to the Chamber which is the high school you completed? That's the first thing.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was a vocational school for an explosives technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did you start working with that factory? Or, rather, ever since you completed your education, you were employed with the factory; is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I began working at the factory in 1972. I worked until the 4th of April 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I began working at the factory in 1982.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have the correct version in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, you produced what?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We were not producing anything but, rather, assembling mines and explosives for the need of the Yugoslav People's Army and for export.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us when you stopped working. Prior to that, who were the people working in the factory? And first and foremost, I wanted to know something about the workers there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If you mean whether there were civilians or military personnel because it was a purpose industry, I would tell you that we were all civilian. There were no military people there. It was just a factory that produced for the needs of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many workers did the factory employ before the war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The entire factory, which was split into several sectors, there were 5.000 to 6.000 people. In the purpose part, which had to do with assembly, some 900 to 1.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In peacetime, where did the products go?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was used by the Yugoslav People's Army, and, pursuant to certain contracts concluded by the Ministry of Defence, for export throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about any distribution in the former republics, when it comes to the former Yugoslavia or, rather, the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: As I said, the factory was directly controlled by the Ministry of Defence and they distributed the products according to their needs. Therefore, I guess the products went to all of the republics, to various storage locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me who the people were who were in charge of certain areas? Who were the people organising things in the factory at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: If you mean the managing staff, those were mainly chemical engineers, ballistics experts, from the civilian sector. Even those who represented the Ministry of Defence during various controls and to take over the products were civilians; that is, the military control sent by the Ministry of Defence also comprised civilians alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacevic, before the break you told us a few things. Among others, you said that you worked in the factory until the 4th of April 1992. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 4th of April 1992, I came to work as usual. However, since there was an incident in the centre of town in front of the government building and the Holiday Inn, many workers failed to appear. We went to the factory restaurant and one of the managers came from the purpose part of the factory and he told us that we were to go home. He also told us that they would call us when it would be necessary for us to return to work. And from that moment on, I didn't go to the factory. If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. After that day, you didn't enter the factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Not as a worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened during that day after the workers had left?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: We went home and waited for someone to call us. The manager told us that it would be broadcast via the media when the workers were supposed to return to their work posts. However, six or seven days passed. In the meantime the Special Police forces of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina entered the premises or, rather, a part of the Special Forces, because by that time the police had already split into the Muslim and the Serb part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which part of the police entered the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The Pretis factory, well, the Muslim part of the police entered the factory. They were commanded by Dragan Vikic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: What happened was that early in the morning, they went through the cargo entrance of the factory. They secured that part of the factory, entered it with some trucks, and took away mines and explosives. We don't know what the quantity was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what type of mines and explosives were there in the factory, considering its production?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The factory had its own warehouses, temporary warehouses, which were never completely full because one batch would leave as another would come in. It would either be sent to the army or for export. You could find all types of products there, everything we produced, classical weaponry, 57 millimetres up to 152 millimetres. As concerns the missile programme, we had 90-millimetre anti-tank rockets, Osa 1 and Osa 2; then we had 128-millimetre rockets called Plamen A, fire A; then 128-millimetre rocket-type Oganj. All those were in the warehouses. On top of that, we also produced parts for Orkan. It was not a part of the serial production. And we also produced aircraft bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was early in the morning. What happened then? Where did the trucks go to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They went towards the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I didn't follow the transcript. I think the witness said aircraft bombs FAB and that is not to be found in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Aircraft bombs FAP, F-A-P? F-A-P or F-A-B?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] B, F-A-B. Your Honours, that wasn't entered into the transcript. I know that this is difficult work for interpreters because of the speed - and we are to be blamed for that - but when we were double-checking the transcript a while ago, we saw that some things were missing. It is impossible for us to react at any given moment to all the omissions. For example, this to us was an important matter and I had no time to pay attention to it. In any case, I will try to speak as slowly as possible and I will ask the witness to pay attention, particularly when mentioning numbers, to the screen so as to see whether everything has been entered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, you should know that the transcript is routinely corrected. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am. But during examination, it creates confusion. I know that it is difficult and that it is revised later. Thank you. Let us proceed slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was in the morning of that day. Did anything else happen that day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That day --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a second. It seems that Judge Harhoff has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, because I didn't fully understand whether the Muslim part of the police took away only mines and explosives or whether they also took all the weaponry that was present in the warehouses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Pretis factory, there was no weaponry, only mines, explosives and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I thought -- I'm just checking the transcript now, but I thought you just told us a while ago that there were all sorts of interesting things in the warehouses. You said that there were all types of products there, "everything we produced, classical weaponry, 57 millimetres up to 152 millimetres." And some "90-millimetre anti-tank rockets, Osa 1 and Osa 2; then we also had 128-millimetre rockets called Plamen," and so on and so forth. All of this, was that also taken by the Muslim police?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Harhoff, this is what I was talking about a moment ago. In my language, he was crystal clear that there was only ammunition produced, that there was no weaponry. You can see for yourself what sort of confusion it can create. He was talking about the fact that they produced ammunition for those types of weaponry, and in the transcript one gathers that the very pieces were there. But this is all ammunition for such weapons. This is the type of misunderstanding we can have. And in the end we would end up with a transcript which would state that there was weaponry of all sorts and kinds there. But this was a factory that produced ammunition for weapons. The only thing that was taken away was ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And all of the ammunition was taken away? That was my question. Witness, was everything emptied from the Pretis factory, including what was to be found in the warehouses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said a moment ago, I don't know what the quantity was. I didn't do the inventory. I don't know about any quantities. Perhaps a part of it was taken away or -- in any case, I don't know how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far is your house from the factory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Three to 4 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The things you just said, could you observe that yourself or was it in your settlement? In any case, how did people know about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is like this: Since it was early in the morning, no one would have known about it. However, after the incursion of the Special Police and after they took away the mines and explosives and ammunition, and then the local Green Berets from Kobilja Glava entered the factory, trying to do the very same thing. But by that time the factory security managed to reorganise and a skirmish ensued. There were wounded. The first time there were two incursions by the Special Forces and the third incursion was an attempt by some armed civilians. The security forces prevented them. One could hear a fire exchange and a few hours later I went to the factory. That's how I found out. I learned that from my co-workers who worked in the security part of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the victims were? You said that there was an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: With our security force, there were no casualties. I think there were some wounded, though; I saw it on TV three or four days later. I saw some wounded lads in the Kosevo Hospital. I don't know what their names are but there are recordings. It was in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain something else to me, but first I need to show you a map and we'll try to depict that for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show a 65 ter document, 02829. It is an UNPROFOR map.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, can you tell the Judges who Vikic was at the time and what he became afterwards.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dragan Vikic at the time, and later as well, was a commander of the Special Police unit of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of operations did they take part in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It is well known what special military or police units are expected to do. In our case, they took part in these riots or sabotage actions and things like that, as far as I knew. But I came across them during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was MUP involved in combat actions as well?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, and I haven't risen to this point, but with respect that goes far, far away from anything set out in this witness's 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was a strictly and explicitly cited incident which bears enormous significance for the army -- for the arming of the army, and it is also strictly mentioned in the summary relating to this witness, and he's talking about the things that deserve your attention. Perhaps this last question, but before that I don't see -- this incursion into the factory by special MUP units and the seizure of weapons was something mentioned in the summary, as something that this witness is going to talk about, and I don't see anything inappropriate in relation to the issue we are facing, especially since he mentioned that there were air bombs that may have been taken on that occasion, among other things.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You want to be heard again, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was in fact the very last question I had risen on, whether or not the MUP was involved in combat actions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, but I'll allow the question. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maunaga, the President allowed this question to be asked.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Kovacevic, not Maunaga.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My apologies. I am a bit senile.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, MUP was directly involved in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be enough. Now, after that incident, the shooting, the seizure of weapons, what happened next? Can you first please show us your house, Vogosca and the factory.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is Vogosca. The factory was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have to put a mark on the map, please, and this will be saved.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The factory is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it's better -- it will be better if you put a circle.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: And this is where my house is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So, please, what happened after these incidents that you have just described, the ones that took place in early April? What did you do? What did other people do? Can you tell us what happened next?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: That was in April. In April, people used to pass through my neighbourhood, expelled from Buca Potok.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slowly give the names of the families.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you first please slowly give the names of the family that had been expelled or left Buca Potok, after you have shown us where this Buca Potok is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is Buca Potok, and the families who fled in April or were expelled from Buca Potok - as far as I know, there were many families - were Odzakovic, Zivkovic, Rakic, Stevanovic. I know about the Stevanovic family. There were two brothers. One of them was injured on that occasion and the other was killed. His name was Milojica Stevanovic and the wounded one was Negos. They all passed through my neighbourhood over the Zuc plateau because that was the only escape route for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw a line along that route.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: They told me that the attack had occurred sometime in the morning, as far as I remember. There was a brief skirmish. Given the fact that the Serb families in the area were heavily outnumbered, there were casualties and there were wounded persons. Those who managed to get across the Zuc plateau escaped. As for those who didn't, I really don't know what became of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please give us a brief and swift account of what happened in May?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, I think early in May, around the 10th of May, the army of Republika Srpska was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, meaning throughout May, the barracks in the centre of Sarajevo remained blocked, under siege. An agreement had been reached for the military to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina by the 19th of May 1992. This agreement was complied with. All the town centre barracks, the Marshal Tito barracks, the Viktor Bubanj barracks, the Jusuf Dzonlic barracks, the Jajce barracks, and the command of the 7th Military District at Bistrik, all those were surrendered to the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood, people started organising themselves under the control of the Territorial Defence Staff. The Rajlovac barracks was being transferred to its eventual destination. They were moving out. So we set up units; rather, the TO staff organised units, armed fighters, using the weapons left over after the JNA had evacuated the Rajlovac barracks. And if I may just finish this, this was a training centre for JNA air forces -- air force. There were no heavy weapons being kept there. Those were just the sort of planes, model planes, used for training and anti-aircraft guns of very small calibre. There were no heavy weapons. If there had been any, the military would have taken it away with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: However, let me ask you something else. After you had organised yourselves, were there any weapons left behind by the JNA outside these barracks in the area? Did you see any other serious weapons?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't myself. I was just an ordinary soldier at the time and I had no information to indicate whether there were any such things lying around. There was no need for me to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So what did those people eventually do? Who were the fighters belonging to those units in your own neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Those were just local residents. Just to clarify matters for both you and the Chamber, this area was an ethnically Serb area. There were no Muslims residing there; not within a 20-kilometre radius, in fact. Therefore, those were locals. The fighters along the front lines were actually standing in front of their own homes, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Before I seek additional explanations about what went on in June, can you just tell us how many people from Buca Potok went on to those places that you indicated? And do you know what was going on in Pofalici in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: People were leaving every day. Nobody knows exactly how many people. This was when the clashes first started and it was still possible to leave the area through the woods, across the Zuc plateau. This area, it's woodlands basically and people kept leaving every day. The previous example that I gave you was because of the attack, because of the clashes. But later on, even when there were no clashes, people were leaving the area. They were feeling unsafe. You're asking me about Pofalici. It was sometime in mid-May, the 15th or the 16th, that Pofalici was attacked. I believe, well, based on my recollection, this was several days after the Marshal Tito barracks had been evacuated. Straight after that Pofalici was evacuated, and this was a predominantly Serb settlement. However, they enjoyed the support of forces from the centre of town itself and they expelled the people living there. I know about the specific cases where the families of some of my friends were killed. One of them, Djordje Elek eventually found the bones belonging to his parents, but Zoran Mikelic [as interpreted] never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. What happened after all of this in June? What happened in the area where you lived and where your neighbours lived? Did any further clashes erupt after that, if you could please explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It's not Zoran Mikelic; it's Pikulic. And Djordje, his last name is Elek. I did say it, didn't I? And now that I remember this, at the beginning of my evidence, it said 1972 instead of 1982, when I started working in that factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you very much. We've now set the record straight. Can you tell us anything about June, please, anything to do with the positions? Was there now a confrontation line there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: From the beginning of 1992 to June 1992, there was a large-scale offensive on Zuc hill, which is where I was deployed at the time as a soldier of the army of Republika Srpska. The offensive continued for two days. On day 2, the morning of day 2, I myself was wounded and taken to Pale, and then from Pale to Belgrade. Therefore, I can't tell you anything about June.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was it that you were wounded? Which part of your body, I mean.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My stomach.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go next? Which route did you take?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, the then-not-international but now-international Sarajevo airport was under the control of the Serb army. I crossed the runway to Lukavica and then from there to Pale and then from Pale by helicopter on to Belgrade. When I returned --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. How long did you stay in hospital for?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: My treatment officially ended on the 8th of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So how did you go back?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I went back through the hills above Sarajevo and not across the runway. The runway had been surrendered to UNPROFOR by this time. So I went back through Pale, through the mountains, through Visevice, Sedrenik, Vogosca, Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems when you eventually reached your home?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, not at the time. But when I went to Sokolac for medical check-ups, I had to take a different route - Pretis, Poljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please just draw a rough line on the map to indicate the route.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's fine. That's fine. All right. Any problems?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this route was under fire permanently because it was near the confrontation lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. All right. You arrived on the 8th of August. Can you please draw the confrontation line separating the army of Republika Srpska on the one hand and the BH army on the other? And I'm referring to your own area, the area in which you lived.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: At the time the confrontation line ran like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. What time are you talking about, after you'd left or once you returned?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Both. The confrontation line remained until the 12th of June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. As of 12th of June 1993, where was it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Just the way it's drawn, the red and yellow lines. They didn't budge until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what were you at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I was -- I was a platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you indicate the place along these confrontation lines drawn there in red and yellow, as you say, where your platoon was positioned.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please put the letter S over that section of the line.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the location of your house with the letter K.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the location of the Pretis factory with a letter L.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please mark Buca Potok with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then the line from Buca Potok to your house with the letter M.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then the blue area with a W.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Who was the commander of your company?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sinisa Krsman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, show me and mark for me - use a different colour - the positions along this confrontation line held at the time by soldiers belonging to that company.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yet another line, right next to it, to mark the area held by the battalion, the battalion that the platoon and companies were subordinated to, naturally.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about towards Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The positions that you held -- geographically, there is no other way for me to ask this question. What was your position in relation to the places held at the time by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was like this: In the area of responsibility of my platoon, this is a mountainous area, woodlands mostly. You can see Zuc hill, a wooded area; that was on my side. And then this line that I marked here, which remained until June 1993, that's in a river valley, and in 1993, it shifted back by about 500 metres. And there was a hill there called Sokolje, which is a continuation, so to speak, of Zuc. It shows that one hill and some houses on the slopes of Sokolje and those were the last houses this side of the hill. And then the confrontation line continued on to the road in Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please draw that for us.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is the road, the highway, and above it is Sokolje hill, which sort of encloses the entire area. And then when the confrontation line went through the barracks, it went underneath the railroad track, while above it there was the highway, the motor road, at a higher altitude. And then the whole settlement, Bielsko Brdo, sort of rises in terms of altitude from the barracks, our line through the barracks and Rajlovac, through the field, through the field. So each and every point was larger in relation to our lines or our positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Points? What points are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: All of our points were lower down in relation to those occupied by the Muslim army, which later became the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just tell me, what exactly could you see from there, from all those positions along the red line, the ones occupied by your battalion throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The line was established back in 1993 and remained throughout the best part of the war. So from my area of responsibility, I saw Zuc hill, Sokolje hill and the wood behind us, as well as the trenches of the Muslim units across the way from us, needless to say. Much in the same way, from the area of responsibility of the battalion, you could see the front row of houses on the slopes and their transfer places.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe briefly how the combat operations looked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was talking about trenches and it says "transfer" on the record, "transfer place." And he was talking about trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Right? Trenches?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How far were your trenches from their trenches?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Depending on the terrain, the distance was normally between 100 metres and 200 or 300 metres in certain places, but it all depended on the lie of the land. Along my own line, the distance was about 100 to 120 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Across the positions, what exactly could you see?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Just the hill and the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when General Dragomir Milosevic became commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I'd be at a loss for the exact date. I know it was late summer, possibly early autumn. I think late summer 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How would you describe the period after he became commander, in terms of any combat operations going on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, as far as 1994 is concerned, I can say this: Following the withdrawal of heavy weapons, there had been an agreement about that. Sometime in February 1994, a cease-fire took effect and it was complied with until the end of that year, winter, possibly October, when an offensive was launched at the Nisic plateau. As a rule, there would be active provocation along our confrontation lines around Rajlovac after that, although we did go and help out with certain parts of the Nisic front at the Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When did that stop?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I think the offensive was first launched in October and ground to a halt by the end of December, I'd say, with small interruptions, brief interruptions. It went on for two months. It was sometime in December. I can't remember if a truce was signed or anything like that, but it did go on until nearly mid-1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Krsman, he was your superior commander; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of orders would you normally get from him in your capacity as platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The orders normally came down to routine matters. There was no need to emphasise that one should be careful using up ammunition, although from our positions we couldn't really fire all that much. We didn't have a clear line of sight to begin with. It was only if we came under an attack and then we would fire back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What if you realised that there was some sort of danger?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It was exactly that type of situation that he addressed. He told us that it was only in this type of situation that we should start firing, when regrouping or, for example, if our positions came under attack or, for example, if we realised that the enemy was bringing in fresh forces. These were the only situations he said in which we should go into action. There were examples like that in my part of the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you always wait for them to start firing first, or given the manoeuvres that were going on all the time, did you sometimes do things yourselves?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Most certainly not. We observed their activities and whenever we realised that they were about to do something, we would open fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. A cease-fire has now been agreed. Do you get any orders from Krsman regarding that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: The orders were passed along orally. He would tour the line and then platoon commanders would meet, company commanders, and he would convey these orders to us orally, to be careful about unnecessary waste of ammunition, not to fire without an order, even when provoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a Defence document. It has been admitted already. It's D214.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, please. Your Honours, could this map be saved the way it is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Can it be saved?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An exhibit, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be admitted as Exhibit D226.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 214, D214, brought up for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the date, please. Can you tell us what it is and can you please tell us what the document is about? Please pay close attention to paragraph 4. And is that the same thing that Sinisa Krsman told you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what I was talking about. He told me not to open fire unless there was a surprise attack, and in any other situation, when we deemed it necessary to open fire, we should first seek approval from the operations centre of the brigade command. That's exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you describe what the situation was like after December and how long the situation continued for, the one that you described.

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: After December, as I said, probably some sort of a cease-fire had been agreed and it literally looked like a cease-fire until sometime in mid-May when all these acts of provocation started, and when we, the soldiers along the front line, started learning about this. At the time, I must say a lot of Serbs managed to leave town. They used their connections; they escaped across the lines. So we had received information to indicate that the BH army was about to launch a full-on offensive, a large-scale offensive. We found out about this sometime in May and then it wasn't before mid-June - I think the 15th or the 16th - that a veritable offensive got off the ground, I think all along the front line, well, certainly along my part, but I know it was all along the front line, all positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But as long as the cease-fire was still on - and we have to finish in several minutes - can you explain about the areas in which you were moving at the time? What exactly was the situation regarding fuel, electricity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't just about that period. This is something that I forgot to say earlier on. In addition to these clashes, the whole war, with the exception of when the power lines, for example, were destroyed during the fighting, the supply never ceased. There was a power station in Rajlovci that supplied electricity to the city and the areas under Serb control. There was the Sarajevo gas station and they could open the supply line or cut off the supplies, but this normally didn't happen because those were all under UNPROFOR control. And then there were the centre warehouses of humanitarian aid for the entire Sarajevo area, and this all ran smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Humanitarian aid warehouses for Serbs and Bosniaks, Muslims, alike was in Rajlovac; right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did it reach its destination?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: Why not? Drivers would pick up shipments at the warehouse; they would load it on to their vehicles and drive it into town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about in the middle of combat, when the power lines were destroyed? What happened then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN KOVACEVIC
utterances.text: I remember this one particular cease-fire. The power lines collapsed on Zuc hill, from artillery fire, so - and they had probably agreed about this - people from the Muslim part of Sarajevo came to fix it, experts, and they worked with our experts to fix the power lines there. And this was sometime late in 1992, the cease-fire that I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we are approaching the end of today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. We will adjourn until tomorrow.
